cards.title: Find a simple closed quasigeodesic in polynomial time
cards.formal: Can one construct, in polynomial time on every convex polyhedron, a nonconstant simple closed curve that is a quasigeodesic at every point of the surface? The geometric target is specified below; the numerical input/output and computation conventions needed to make “polynomial time” a complete benchmark remain unresolved in this imported formulation.
cards.why: Would turn a classical geometric existence theorem into an efficient constructive procedure.

progress.text: Pogorelov proves the geometric existence theorem, as recounted in the checked sources.
A finite geometric algorithm is given, with a weak-simplicity target and an explicit degenerate-case convention in the convex discussion.
The corrected related algorithm separates real and word models and bounds its output segment count pseudopolynomially.

cards.definitions: A convex polyhedron here is a compact convex polytope K⊂ℝ³ with nonempty interior, whose boundary ∂K is a polyhedral sphere. Distances and angles are intrinsic to that boundary: neighboring faces may be unfolded into a plane along a shared edge. A simple closed curve is a continuous injective map γ:S¹→∂K, where S¹ is a circle; equivalently, a parametrization on [0,1] has equal endpoints and no other repetitions. The curve is nonconstant and locally polygonal. At a point away from a polyhedron vertex it must become a straight line after local unfolding. At a vertex on the curve, its two incident directions divide the total incident face angle into two surface angles, each required to be at most π. These angles are measured along the surface, not as angles of 3D chords. An ordinary geodesic has angle π on both sides everywhere; the relaxed condition allows a quasigeodesic to pass through a vertex with positive angular defect. The desired output is one curve satisfying all these conditions, not an approximate curve or an existence certificate without a specified curve. A doubled path that retraces itself is not injective and is excluded from this imported strict-simple target.
cards.answer_criterion: After the missing numerical and output conventions are fixed from the intended source model, exhibit one uniform algorithm with a polynomial worst-case bound in that model’s input size, or prove that no such algorithm exists. A finite but geometrically dependent exponential procedure, a possibly self-intersecting quasigeodesic or a weakly simple doubled path does not satisfy the stated strict polynomial-time target. The current card is not marked as a completed standalone computational formulation.

context_blocks.title: A straight route on a folded surface
context_blocks.text: A route can turn sharply in three-dimensional space when it crosses a polyhedron edge yet be straight after the two faces are unfolded. At an actual vertex, less than a full turn of surface may be available, so the two-sided angle condition replaces ordinary straightness. On a cube, the square loop halfway up the four vertical faces unfolds locally straight and is a simple closed geodesic.

context_blocks.title: Existence and finding a curve
context_blocks.text: Pogorelov’s classical theorem supplies simple closed quasigeodesics on convex polyhedra. Turning that existence statement into a fast construction requires controlling both the number of face segments and the exact geometry of their endpoints. A bound involving a ratio of geometric lengths can be enormous compared with the number of bits needed to describe those lengths.

context_blocks.title: What the 2022 algorithm actually guarantees
context_blocks.text: Chartier and de Mesmay give a finite algorithm for weakly simple closed quasigeodesics on polyhedral spheres, with running time exponential in the number of vertices and a length-to-altitude ratio. Their convex-case discussion also permits a doubled path between two vertices as a degenerate simple case. That convention needs explicit attention when comparing the theorem with a request for an injective loop.

context_blocks.title: Later work keeps the model important
context_blocks.text: The October 2025 revision by Demaine, Hesterberg and Ku corrects earlier details and separates real-RAM bounds from word-RAM bounds for radical-expression inputs. It also gives a pseudopolynomial bound on the number of face visits. The 2025 cube classification concerns one special polyhedron. Neither checked result supplies the general polynomial algorithm requested here.

context_blocks.title: The remaining formulation gap
context_blocks.text: The geometric request is now explicit. The source import still needs one precise convention for representing the polyhedron and the exact output curve, and for charging arithmetic operations. Those choices affect the meaning of polynomial time. This gap is recorded instead of treating a newly chosen numerical variant as the original question.

statement_review.remaining_issue: The imported polynomial-time request does not select a numerical input encoding, exact output representation or operation-cost model. cards.title: Three-page book embedding with a fixed vertex order
cards.formal: Is there a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm that, given a finite simple undirected graph G and a fixed linear order ≺ of V(G), decides whether its edges can be partitioned into at most three pages, with no two edges on one page having alternating endpoints in ≺?
cards.why: The smallest unresolved page count in a canonical graph layout and circle-graph coloring problem.

progress.text: The cited book-embedding paper distinguishes the fixed-order two-page and four-page complexity results.
A published examination identifies flaws in the earlier claimed polynomial circle-graph 3-coloring algorithm.
A SOSA algorithm establishes a quasipolynomial upper bound for circle-graph 3-coloring and fixed-order three-page embedding.

cards.definitions: The input is n≥0, the adjacency matrix of G on vertices [n], and a permutation listing every vertex exactly once in the prescribed order; let N be the total binary input length. The order is part of the input and may not be changed. A page assignment is a function c:E(G)→{1,2,3}, with unused pages allowed. Two edges {a,b} and {x,y}, oriented so a≺b and x≺y, alternate exactly when a≺x≺b≺y or x≺a≺y≺b. These inequalities are strict: edges sharing an endpoint do not conflict, and nested edges are permitted. A valid assignment gives different page numbers to every alternating pair. The algorithm must answer yes exactly when such an assignment exists and no otherwise, on every input; there is no promise of planarity or a restricted graph class. Polynomial time means one deterministic Turing machine and constants C,k, independent of the graph and order, with at most C(N+1)^k steps. The number of pages is the fixed constant three, not an input parameter. Graphs without edges are yes instances.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the existence of the stated uniformly polynomial, always-correct decision algorithm, or prove that no such algorithm exists. An NP-hardness reduction gives a negative conclusion only under the corresponding assumption P≠NP; a quasipolynomial algorithm gives an upper bound but does not prove polynomial solvability. This yes/no formulation follows the polynomial-time question explicitly retained by the current primary source.

context_blocks.title: Pages prevent crossings
context_blocks.text: Place the vertices along the spine of a book in the given order and put each edge inside one page. Edges whose endpoints alternate would cross if put together. For 1≺2≺3≺4, edges {1,3} and {2,4} conflict, whereas {1,4} and {2,3} are nested and can share a page. Three pages give three choices for each edge.

context_blocks.title: Why circle-graph coloring appears
context_blocks.text: Make a conflict graph H with one vertex for each edge of G and adjacency exactly for alternating pairs. A page assignment is then a proper three-coloring of H. Such conflict graphs are circle graphs: graphs represented by crossings of chords with distinct endpoints on a circle. Shared spine vertices can be separated into nearby chord endpoints without creating extra conflicts. Conversely, a chord diagram gives an ordered matching, so the two computational problems have polynomial reductions.

context_blocks.title: The exceptional page count
context_blocks.text: With one page, one only checks for conflicting edges. With two pages, the conflict graph must be bipartite, which is polynomial-time decidable. Four pages already give an NP-complete problem. The three-page case lies between these understood cases; results that choose the spine order address a different input model.

context_blocks.title: A corrected history and a new upper bound
context_blocks.text: An older claimed polynomial algorithm for three-coloring circle graphs does not establish the result: Bachmann, Rutter and Stumpf identify concrete correctness defects. The SOSA 2026 algorithm gives time h^{O(log h)} for a circle graph with h vertices, and hence quasipolynomial time for this ordered-graph problem. Its exponent grows logarithmically with input size, so it leaves the fixed-exponent polynomial-time question open.

sentences: Vertices are fixed along a line, and each edge must be assigned to one of three pages.
Two edges with alternating endpoints cannot share a page, while nested edges and shared endpoints are allowed.
The question asks whether feasibility can always be decided in deterministic polynomial time.
It is equivalent to three-coloring circle graphs, where a prior claimed polynomial algorithm has known defects.
A SOSA 2026 quasipolynomial algorithm advances the upper bound but leaves polynomial-time solvability open.

meta.status_scope: No claim of exhaustive open-status verification
methodology: Detailed cards have individually written statements, context, significance, and documented results. Source notes are unfinished research records and do not yet meet that standard. The legacy index is retained for traceability.
Open in the source means open at the date of that source. The build date, 10 September 2026, does not establish current open status. Old excerpts may omit conditions or subsequent results.

Selection considers model power, necessary resources, sharp bounds, structural characterizations, explicit constructions, and minimal assumptions. Source notes use a heuristic screen; detailed cards give an individual explanation.

The earlier automatic paper screen allowed at most one new card per paper title and rejected identical formulations and close duplicates within a source. Approved textbook and survey imports retain multiple distinct questions per publication. Confirmed overlaps supplement existing cards; collection-wide semantic deduplication remains incomplete.

Short quotations retain the source language. Later related literature, where listed, is a research aid rather than evidence of resolution. Personal notes and saved cards are stored locally in your browser.

Textbook and survey questions are dated paraphrases; source locations, conjectures, research directions and caveats are preserved on the problem cards. These annotations do not establish current open status or change a later card review. New source drafts remain unassessed for importance. The reader contains the imported questions and external bibliographic references only; source files are not bundled.

Selection groups follow the agreed 10 large and 25 small categories. We aim for benchmarks of 100 and 500 problems, with a possible expansion to 1,000. All three use the same category order and the same ranking within each category. The respective prefixes are 5/2, 25/10 and 50/20 problems per large/small category. The possible 1,000-problem expansion has 1000 assigned places and 0 reserved places. Each card records its category explicitly. These counts describe saved candidates; classification does not verify a statement or its current open status. Deleted records are absent from the catalogue and exports. Their stable IDs and reasons are retained to prevent reimport. Final quota selection and a comprehensive deduplication audit remain pending.

Importance ordering is an editorial assessment of foundational significance, breadth of consequences, and influence on other questions. Each assessed card gives a reason. The category-wide review also uses shared priority bands for questions of comparable scope; it does not claim that these ties have a scientifically meaningful internal order. Unassessed drafts share a provisional score of 50; their relative order is only an ID tie-break, not an importance judgment. The first 5/2 places in each large/small category are an explicit editorial focus selection balancing importance and topical diversity. Focus ordering does not alter importance scores; remaining candidates use score and ID order. The targets are 100 and 500 problems, with a possible expansion to 1,000. Top 100, Top 500 and the possible Top 1000 use the first 5/2, 25/10 and 50/20 category places respectively, all from the same ranking. Category positions include all candidates and remain fixed when filtering. Publication date, source date, and card detail do not increase importance. Records marked resolved are placed after the remaining candidates, without changing their historical importance score. Importance review does not establish that a saved question is still open.
